payload.name: Modality effect
payload.fact: Replacing visual text with spoken text increases the effectiveness of multimedia instructions in terms of better learning results or less mental effort spent.

provenance.title: Multimedia instructions and cognitive load theory: Effects of modality and cueing
provenance.quote_or_locus: replacing visual text with spoken text (the modality effect) and adding visual cues relating elements of a picture to the text (the cueing effect) both increase the effectiveness of multimedia instructions in terms of better learning results or less mental effort spent

decision_note: Inverted. The sole cited paper (Tabbers, Martens & van Merrienboer 2004) found the OPPOSITE of this fact. The quoted span at offsets 369-638 sits in the abstract's BACKGROUND section, where the paper restates what cognitive load theory and Mayer's theory PREDICT. Its own RESULTS report that replacing visual text with spoken text produced LOWER retention and transfer scores, and CONCLUSIONS names the finding 'a reverse modality effect', attributed to the instructions being learner-paced rather than system-paced. The model quoted the paper accurately, from the part of the paper the paper went on to refute. This is not a weak effect to be downgraded: an effect whose only source reports its reversal is evidence against, and filing it at any grade would put a false claim in the registry under a humble-looking label. Approving the reverse effect instead would need a fresh extraction anchored to the RESULTS span, not an edit of this one.
